prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, with which independent laboratories compare optical frequencies at the 10^-18 level
for the discovery of iron-based high-temperature superconductors

statement.case_for: I keep my round-1 configuration, and the exchange has made me more certain of the reasons rather than of the count. Part one, the optical lattice clock (Katori, Ye), is an invention in the sense of the statutes: a specific idea, the magic-wavelength trap that cancels the light shift of the clock transition while many atoms sit in the Lamb-Dicke regime, proposed and first realised by Katori in 2001-2003, and then carried by Ye's group to the 10^-18 regime and to many-body clocks. The result is verified in the way I trust most, by independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, SYRTE, PTB, NIST, NPL) reproducing and intercomparing it, and it has already been used to measure the gravitational redshift over a millimetre and to bound drifting constants. To answer the chair's question in one sentence: the frequency comb of 2005 made optical frequencies countable and the 2012 prize honoured control of a single trapped quantum system, whereas the lattice clock is the first scheme that interrogates a large ensemble of neutral atoms without a trap-induced shift, which is why it overtook the ion clocks in stability and why it opens new measurements. Part two, Hosono, is an original experimental discovery, the 2008 observation of superconductivity near 26 K in fluorine-doped LaFeAsO, reproduced within weeks worldwide, now eighteen years old, with attribution to one laboratory leader that I find unusually clean. I propose the second citation to read as a discovery of a family of materials, not a record temperature. Three people in total, two separate achievements, both mature and experimentally verified.
statement.case_against: The pairing has no common thread, as Danielsson himself says, and a purist may call two unrelated parts a compromise. If the committee prefers a single coherent subject, B040 alone is a perfectly defensible prize and I would not regard it as a failure of my position; my reason for a second part is that Hosono's discovery is clean, verified and old enough that waiting adds nothing, and I do not think it should be held back merely because no other part in the slate is a natural companion. Against B040 itself: the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes remains a judgment call, the redefinition of the second has not been adopted, and I cannot rule out that Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Lemonde or Takamoto have a claim I have not verified; the chair's request for external expert reports on Tokyo versus JILA priority has not been answered in anything I have read. Against B028: the pairing mechanism is still unexplained, the early Tc increases to 55 K were achieved by other groups, and Kamihara, the first author of the 2008 paper, is outside a one-name credit; Hosono has only two committee supporters.

responses.point: Kroll argues that B040 is a clean idea turned into a reproducible instrument, intercompared across many national laboratories at 1e-18, that it beat ion clocks in stability because it interrogates many atoms at once, and that the pending redefinition of the second is procedural and not a question of whether the physics works.
responses.response: I agree with the evidence he relies on, and the intercomparison is the point that matters most to an experimentalist: the result is not one group's claimed record but something reproduced by several. I also accept that the redefinition is procedural and I would not make the prize wait for it. Where I am still not fully satisfied is the two-name credit, since you list Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Lemonde and Takamoto as genuine contributors. I would ask you to say whether Katori's first strontium lattice clock demonstration and the later Ye-group accuracy work are separable enough that no other individual has a claim of comparable weight. If you can, I am content with Katori and Ye. The one point I would put in the citation is that the invention is the lattice scheme and its development, which keeps it distinct from the comb.

responses.point: Danielsson pairs B040 with Hosono, agrees the unresolved pairing mechanism is no reason to wait, and wants the citation to credit the discovery of the family and not the Tc record given the rapid extension to 55 K by Chinese groups.
responses.response: I agree on the citation: the original observation is superconductivity in the iron arsenide family, and the later records are developments by others, which is why I propose wording that does not mention transition temperature. On your own reservation that the pairing is an arbitrary combination, I do not think it should be hidden. We are proposing two unrelated achievements and the committee should say so openly. What I would resist is letting the lack of a common thread decide the matter, since the statutes ask whether each part is a discovery or invention of importance. Where I differ slightly is on Kamihara: as first author he has a claim, and I would like us to check the 2006 LaFePO and 2008 papers before we call the credit clean.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B061 alone and argues that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap can be handled by a citation built on the prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and its first observation, that 2016 covered phase transitions and not the time-reversal-invariant class, and that Krivanek's absence from B046 is a comparable gap.
responses.response: His comparison with B046 is fair, and it is one reason I did not put B046 first. On 2016 I now accept that the overlap is partial, and I withdraw the suggestion that it is duplication. I still do not agree that citation wording repairs the gap. The HgTe experiment was designed from the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, so leaving them out is not like leaving out a later improver, it is leaving out the author of the specific prediction that the experimentalists tested. If the committee names Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, a reader will ask who made the prediction that Molenkamp measured. That is exactly the question about who did the original work, and I cannot be absolutely sure of the answer. I keep B061 as my first alternative but not as my preferred part.

responses.point: Lindroth defends the lattice clock as a discovery-grade result, not only an instrument, because it produced new gravitational redshift and constants measurements, and says that if the committee wanted an even-handed attribution of the TEM and STEM branches she would rank B046 below B040.
responses.response: I accept her consistency argument and her ranking of B046 below B040 is one I can now share: with Krivanek outside the trio and no other supporter, I cannot be sure that Rose, Haider and Urban are the full set, so I keep B046 only as a second alternative. I also take her request for a test from outside AMO seriously. From my side, as a microscopist, what persuades me is that the lattice clock passed the test that matters to me, independent reproduction with new measurements enabled, and that it is a tool that opened a door, in the same sense as the 2023 attosecond prize.

uncertainties: Early priority between Katori's group in Tokyo and JILA for the lattice scheme and first strontium clock, and whether Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde, Bloom or Takamoto hold a claim of comparable weight; I have not seen the external expert reports the chair mentions.
Whether a prize with two unrelated parts (clock and iron-based superconductors) is something the committee is willing to defend, as against B040 alone.
Whether Kamihara's role as first author of the 2008 LaFeAsO paper and the 2006 LaFePO work should affect the one-name credit for Hosono.
Whether the redefinition of the second, still pending, should be treated as procedural or as a sign that the lattice clock is not yet fully recognised in practice.
statement.conflict_note: I am an electron microscopist and division head at Chalmers. B046 (aberration-corrected electron microscopy) is in my own field, which is why I do not make it a preferred part and have kept it only as a second alternative; I will not argue for it on the final ballot beyond the attribution concerns already stated. Göran Johansson is also at Chalmers Physics, but his preferred B040 coincides with mine and no preferred part of mine falls in his specialty. I have no recorded tie to Katori, Ye or Hosono. No change from round 1 and no recusal is needed for the preferred parts.
